I have been working this 6 mu of land in Quzhou for 28 years, so I know every corner of it. With six mouths to feed at home, I have to make the most of every mu. My cabbage-chili rotation has always given the steadiest income, so I will put 3.5 mu into spring cabbage this year and follow it with summer chili on the same plots after the cabbage comes off. I will plant 1.5 mu to eggplant because it bears for a long season and the market price stays decent. The remaining 1 mu will go to kidney bean—my family likes it, it fixes a bit of nitrogen, and I can sell whatever we do not eat. I always buy hybrid seeds for cabbage, chili, and eggplant; the germination is uniform and the disease resistance saves me trouble later. For kidney bean, an improved local variety is enough. I use rotary tillage for all crops because it makes the fine seedbeds vegetables need here on the North China Plain. I have a well, so I can irrigate when the spring drought hits or when the summer heat peaks, but I do not water blindly because pumping costs labor and diesel. I apply fertilizer based on what I have watched work year after year: cabbage needs a strong base, chili needs plenty of potassium for fruit set, eggplant is hungry throughout its long season, and kidney bean does not need as much. Chili and eggplant will need the most pesticide sprays because thrips, mites, and shoot borers are relentless around here, while cabbage and bean are easier to keep clean.
